exam: IISER Aptitude Test (IAT) 2027 preparation — provisional 2026-pattern pilot
title: IAT New Test 3
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Fresh original AI-assisted authorship to the 25-test plan and revised IAT instructions; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An alga has phycoerythrin, stores floridean starch and lacks motile reproductive cells. Which class is supported by all three observations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rhodophyceae.
Why: Red algae commonly possess phycoerythrin and store floridean starch. The lack of flagellated reproductive stages supplies a third consistent clue, so classification does not rest on visible colour alone. These three independent traits are more diagnostic than apparent colour alone, which can vary with lighting or accessory pigments. Their combination also excludes a land-plant life cycle.
Why not the others: (A) Green algae characteristically store starch and chlorophyll predominates. (B) Brown algae have fucoxanthin and laminarin/mannitol reserves. (D) Bryophytes are embryophyte land plants, not this algal class.
Key point: Combine pigments, storage material and life-cycle characters.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: In a young root, radial xylem and phloem lie inside a cell layer whose radial walls contain a suberin-rich Casparian strip. What does that layer chiefly regulate?
options: A) Apoplastic entry into the stele by forcing selective membrane crossing
B) Photosynthetic gas exchange in mesophyll
C) Longitudinal phloem pressure from leaf to sink
D) Direct pollen transfer to a stigma
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Endodermal selective entry.
Why: Water moving through cell walls encounters the waterproof strip at the endodermis. To pass inward toward the stele, it must cross a living membrane, where transport can be regulated. The radial vascular arrangement and wall band identify the location. The strip blocks the apoplastic wall route at a continuous endodermal boundary. Water and solutes must enter a symplast through selective membranes before reaching the vascular stele.
Why not the others: (B) Mesophyll is in leaves. (C) Phloem transport occurs after vascular entry and is not the strip's role. (D) Is reproductive transport unrelated to roots.
Key point: Relate wall modification to the path water must take.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A carrier imports Na⁺ and glucose together even when cellular glucose is higher than outside. Blocking the ATP-driven Na⁺ pump eventually stops glucose entry, although the carrier remains present. What powers uptake?
options: B) Direct ATP hydrolysis at the glucose carrier is established by the result
C) Simple diffusion through membrane lipid
D) The Na⁺ gradient maintained by the pump drives coupled glucose transport
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Coupling to the Na⁺ gradient.
Why: Glucose travels uphill, so passive diffusion cannot explain it. The pump uses ATP to maintain a downhill Na⁺ gradient; cotransport can harness that gradient. Blocking the pump removes the stored gradient over time even while the cotransporter protein remains. The Na⁺ gradient provides free energy for cotransport, while ATP is consumed indirectly by the pump that maintains that gradient. Blocking the pump eventually collapses the driver even if the carrier itself still exists.
Why not the others: (A) Glucose is stipulated uphill. (B) The data do not show ATP acting directly on this carrier. (C) Lipid diffusion neither couples Na⁺ nor sustains uphill glucose movement.
Key point: Distinguish direct ATP use from gradient-mediated secondary transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Identical illuminated leaves have equal stomatal aperture and leaf temperature. X is in humid air and Y in dry air, with equal air movement. Initially, which loses more water vapour and why?
options: A) X, because humid air pulls vapour more strongly
B) Y, because its outward vapour-pressure difference is larger
C) Both equally, because aperture alone sets diffusion
D) Neither, because transpiration requires darkness
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Y in dry air.
Why: Water vapour is near saturation in internal leaf spaces. Lower external humidity creates a larger concentration or vapour-pressure gradient through otherwise similar stomata, increasing outward diffusion initially. Holding temperature, aperture and movement constant isolates humidity. Transpiration follows the vapour-pressure gradient from moist internal spaces to outside air. Equal stomatal aperture holds pore conductance approximately fixed, isolating the external humidity difference.
Why not the others: (A) Humidity reduces the gradient. (C) Equal aperture does not eliminate a changed driving difference. (D) Light is present and darkness is not required.
Key point: Flux depends on both conductance and driving gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two tissues receive blood of the same arterial oxygen content. Tissue Q produces more CO₂ and has lower local pH than P. What haemoglobin response helps deliver oxygen to Q?
options: A) Higher pH at Q prevents release
B) Haemoglobin loses all binding capacity permanently
C) Lower pH favours unloading at a given oxygen partial pressure
D) CO₂ creates additional oxygen in blood
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Enhanced oxygen unloading.
Why: More CO₂ and acidity shift haemoglobin's oxygen dissociation relation toward lower affinity. At the same local oxygen pressure, more bound oxygen can therefore be released to metabolically active Q. This is a reversible local response, not destruction of haemoglobin. At the same pO₂ a right-shifted curve has lower saturation, so more oxygen can leave the blood in metabolically active tissue. The higher CO₂ is a local consequence of respiration, not a change in arterial delivery.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the stated pH change. (B) Falsely makes modulation permanent. (D) CO₂ does not synthesize oxygen.
Key point: Relate metabolic CO₂ production to oxygen delivery.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Bagged flowers of P set no seed after hand self-pollination, but set seed after compatible cross-pollination. P's pollen works on another compatible plant. What inference is supported by these controls?
options: A) Failure is specific to the self combination, consistent with self-incompatibility
B) All P pollen is universally nonviable
C) P ovules never develop following fertilisation
D) Bagging always prevents seed formation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Self-combination rejection.
Why: Cross pollen produces seed on P, establishing that its ovules and bagging procedure can support reproduction. P pollen succeeds elsewhere, establishing viability. The remaining contrast is the self combination, consistent with a self-incompatibility response. The cross-pollination control shows the stigma, ovules and bagging method can produce seeds. Failure only with self pollen supports a self-recognition barrier rather than sterility or accidental damage.
Why not the others: (B) Contradicts successful P pollen use. (C) Contradicts cross seed set. (D) Bagged hand crossing worked.
Key point: Reciprocal controls isolate partner specificity from general infertility.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Transcription direction and antiparallel DNA strands
questions.question: The figure shows a short DNA duplex and a promoter arrow pointing right to left. Assume transcription starts at the rightmost shown base, uses the strand read 3′→5′, and ends after the shown sequence. Which mRNA is made, written 5′→3′?
questions.image_alt: Top strand is 5′-TTA CGA CAT-3′ from left to right; bottom strand is 3′-AAT GCT GTA-5′. A promoter arrow at the right points leftward.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5′-AUG UCG UAA-3′.
Why: Moving right to left, polymerase must read a 3′→5′ template, which is the top strand in this orientation. Reverse its base order to TAC AGC ATT, then make the complementary RNA AUG UCG UAA. Equivalently, read the bottom coding strand right to left and replace T by U. Both direction and complementarity matter. The top strand is read in its 3′→5′ direction only when moving from right to left. Complementary RNA is synthesized 5′→3′; reverse the written order before replacing template bases with RNA complements.
Why not the others: (A) Copies the displayed top strand in the wrong direction. (B) Copies the bottom strand left to right. (C) reverses without making the RNA complement.
Key point: Select template by promoter direction before transcribing antiparallel bases.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A person loses many helper T lymphocytes while neutrophil numbers initially remain normal. Which impairment best follows from the helper-cell role?
options: A) Only clot formation is lost
B) Coordination of both antibody and cell-mediated adaptive responses weakens
C) All pathogens immediately stop dividing
D) Innate neutrophils become the sole source of antigen-specific antibodies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Broad adaptive coordination weakens.
Why: Helper T cells signal to other immune cells, including B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Their sustained loss can thus impair both antibody production and cell-mediated responses even when a neutrophil count is initially normal. A count of one innate cell type does not replace adaptive coordination. Helper T-cell signals coordinate antibody production and cellular immunity. Normal neutrophil count does not restore antigen-specific B-cell help, so broad adaptive responses become weaker.
Why not the others: (A) Clotting is not the central helper-cell function. (C) No immune loss sterilises every pathogen. (D) Neutrophils do not secrete antigen-specific antibody.
Key point: Trace effects through the cells a helper population coordinates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: PCR tubes X and Y have the same template, polymerase, nucleotides and cycling. X has both primers flanking a target; Y lacks the reverse primer. What follows for the defined double-stranded target after many ideal cycles?
options: A) Y must amplify the bounded target more rapidly
B) Both amplify exponentially at the same rate
C) X can amplify it exponentially; Y cannot sustain that bounded two-primer process
D) Neither can extend any DNA strand
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Exponential amplification requires both primers.
Why: Opposed primers define both ends and allow newly synthesized target strands to serve as templates on subsequent cycles. With one missing primer, extension from the remaining primer may occur, but the same bounded double-stranded product cannot repeatedly generate itself by two-primer cycling. Each primer binds an opposite template strand with a 3′ end directed into the target interval. One missing primer permits only linear copying of one side, whereas two define products that amplify exponentially.
Why not the others: (A) Missing a primer does not improve target amplification. (B) Overlooks the second defined end. (D) One primer can still support some extension.
Key point: Distinguish any extension from exponential amplification of a defined amplicon.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A plant community has 1000 units net production in an interval. Herbivores consume 250 units and 100 units remain as unconsumed plant biomass; all the rest enters detritus. How many units enter detritus?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 650 units.
Given: The prompt partitions net production into consumption, retained biomass and detritus.
Formula/Principle: Conservation under the stated exhaustive partition.
Step 1: Accounted elsewhere=250+100=350 units.
Step 2: Detritus=1000−350=650 units.
Why: Detritus is not identical to every unconsumed unit because some plant material remains stored during the interval. Net production is already after producer respiration. The stem explicitly partitions it into herbivore consumption, retained biomass and detritus, so subtract exactly the first two non-detrital flows.
Why not the others: (B) ignores stored biomass; (C) ignores herbivory; (D) adds a flow to net production.
Key point: Check whether categories overlap before subtracting.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Pigment needs two independent functional enzymes encoded by A and B; aa or bb blocks the pathway. Two AaBb plants cross. What fraction of offspring is pigmented under complete dominance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9/16.
Given: Pigment requires A_ and B_ together.
Formula/Principle: Independent segregation allows multiplication of the two dominant-phenotype probabilities.
Step 1: Each Aa×Aa locus gives functional phenotype probability 3/4.
Step 2: Both present=(3/4)²=9/16.
Why: Either homozygous recessive block prevents the final pigment even if the other enzyme is present. The pathway is sequential: product from the A-controlled step is substrate for the B-controlled step. A functioning enzyme at only one step cannot bypass the missing other step.
Why not the others: (A) checks only one locus; (B) treats two recessive classes as the requirement; (C) is the white fraction.
Key point: Follow the whole sequential pathway, not one gene alone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In strain P, a functional repressor cannot bind its mutated operator; promoter and structural genes work. Strain Q has a normal operator and repressor. With no glucose, compare enzyme expression without and with lactose.
options: A) Both express only without lactose
B) P expresses in both; Q is low without lactose and induced with it
C) P is always off; Q is always on
D) Both remain off because a promoter is present
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P constitutive, Q inducible.
Why: In P the repressor cannot occupy its DNA site even without inducer, so transcription is not blocked by this control. In Q, bound repressor suppresses transcription until lactose-derived inducer reduces its binding. With glucose absent, the comparison isolates the operator–repressor response rather than catabolite effects. The operator is a cis-acting DNA site, whereas the repressor protein acts in trans. An operator mutation can make a functional repressor unable to block that operon's structural-gene transcription.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses induction. (C) Reverses both strain behaviours. (D) A working promoter permits transcription rather than forbidding it.
Key point: Separate a defective DNA binding site from a defective protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Presynaptic stimulation releases normal transmitter in two preparations. A postsynaptic response occurs in P but not Q; direct electrical stimulation of Q's postsynaptic membrane still gives a normal action potential. Where is the likely defect?
options: B) Axonal action-potential generation in Q's postsynaptic membrane
C) Postsynaptic transmitter reception or coupling
D) Complete absence of the presynaptic neuron
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Postsynaptic reception or coupling.
Why: Normal measured release argues against presynaptic failure. Direct electrical stimulation shows that the postsynaptic membrane can still generate an action potential. The missing response lies between arrival of transmitter and electrical activation, such as receptor binding or its coupling to channels. The presynaptic transmitter measurement rules out a failure of release. A response to direct stimulation confirms downstream excitability, narrowing the lesion to transmitter recognition or the postsynaptic receptor process.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) contradict normal transmitter release. (B) contradicts successful direct electrical activation.
Key point: Use a bypass experiment to localise a failure in a signalling chain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Replication before the two meiotic divisions
questions.question: In ordinary meiosis, when does chromosome DNA replication occur relative to meiosis I and II?
options: A) Once before meiosis I, without replication between the divisions
D) Never, because chromosomes are already visible
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Replication precedes meiosis I only.
Why: S phase copies each chromosome into sister chromatids before homologues separate in the first division. Meiosis II separates those sisters without a second intervening DNA-replication round, allowing haploid products. DNA synthesis occurs once during the preceding interphase. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids without another intervening S phase.
Why not the others: (B) Would duplicate DNA again between divisions. (C) Comes too late for segregation. (D) Visible chromosomes have already been replicated.
Key point: Distinguish one replication from two consecutive divisions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure shows one inherited marker in mother M, child C and candidates P and Q. Assume one allele from each biological parent, precise band sizing and no mutation. What follows from this marker alone?
options: A) Q is established as father with certainty
B) P is compatible and Q excluded, but P is not uniquely proved by one marker
C) Both are excluded because C shares a band with M
D) Each candidate is certainly a parent because each has two bands
questions.image_alt: Gel lanes show M bands 120 and 150, child C 120 and 180, candidate P 160 and 180, and Q 120 and 160, with labelled band-size ladder.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P compatible, Q excluded.
Why: The child can inherit 120 from M; the 180 allele must then come from the other biological parent. P has 180 and Q does not, so Q is excluded under the assumptions. Many untested people might carry 180, so a single marker cannot establish P uniquely. Every child band must be assigned to a parent under the stated single-marker assumptions. The 180 band cannot be supplied by M, so compare that band, rather than overall resemblance, with candidate lanes.
Why not the others: (A) Q lacks 180. (C) Sharing a maternal allele is expected. (D) Two bands alone show neither transmission nor identity.
Key point: A marker may exclude a candidate without proving another uniquely.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Each C–O bond in CO₂ is polar. Under its linear geometry, what is the molecule's net dipole moment?
options: A) Equal to one bond dipole
B) Zero because equal opposite bond dipoles cancel
C) Twice one bond dipole along the same direction
D) Undefined because carbon is central
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zero.
Why: The two identical bond dipole vectors lie on the same line but point in opposite directions from the central carbon. Vector addition cancels them even though each individual C–O bond remains polar. Molecular polarity depends on geometry as well as bond polarity. Each C–O bond contributes an equal dipole in an opposite direction along the O=C=O axis. Vector addition gives \(\boldsymbol\mu_{\rm net}=\boldsymbol\mu_1+\boldsymbol\mu_2=0\), even though individual bonds are polar.
Why not the others: (A) Keeps only one bond. (C) Adds magnitudes without directions. (D) A central atom does not prevent vector addition.
Key point: Sum bond dipoles as vectors.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows small octahedral splitting for complex X and large splitting for Y, both d⁶ at the same metal oxidation state. Under the simple crystal-field model, how many unpaired electrons do X and Y have?
questions.image_alt: Two octahedral energy diagrams have three lower t2g and two upper eg levels; X has gap Δsmall less than pairing energy, Y gap Δlarge greater than pairing energy. No electrons are drawn.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Four and zero.
Why: The small splitting in X makes occupation of the upper eg levels preferable to pairing too early: high-spin d⁶ is t₂g⁴e_g², with four unpaired electrons. The large gap in Y favours pairing in t₂g first: t₂g⁶e_g⁰ has no unpaired electrons. The figure supplies the energetic comparison but leaves the filling to be reasoned out. For d⁶, the high-spin small-gap arrangement leaves more electrons unpaired in both lower and upper sets; the large-gap case pairs in t₂g first. Compare crystal-field energy cost with pairing energy, not merely total d-electron count.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses complexes. (B) Counts only eg electrons in X and invents unpaired electrons in Y. (C) Treats all six d electrons as independently unpaired despite only five orbitals.
Key point: Compare Δ with pairing energy before filling orbitals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Half-filled d subshell in common ions
questions.question: Between Mn²⁺ (Z=25) and Fe²⁺ (Z=26), which has a half-filled 3d subshell and how many 3d electrons does it contain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mn²⁺, 3d⁵.
Why: Neutral Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s² and neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². Forming 2+ ions removes the two 4s electrons first, leaving Mn²⁺ 3d⁵ and Fe²⁺ 3d⁶. Five d electrons give a half-filled five-orbital subshell. The 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons for these cations. Thus Mn²⁺ remains 3d⁵ while Fe²⁺ becomes 3d⁶; only the former has the half-filled d subshell.
Why not the others: (B) Assigns Mn's count to Fe. (C) Retains 4s electrons as 3d. (D) Correctly counts Fe but six is not half-filled.
Key point: Remove ns electrons before (n−1)d in these cations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why is first ionisation energy of N higher than O, despite O's larger nuclear charge?
options: A) Nitrogen has a complete 2p⁶ subshell
C) Oxygen has a paired 2p orbital with extra repulsion relative to N's 2p³ arrangement
D) Nitrogen's outer electrons occupy n=3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Pairing repulsion in O.
Why: N has one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals, a relatively stable half-filled arrangement. O adds a fourth 2p electron that pairs in one orbital; repulsion makes removal of one electron easier than a simple nuclear-charge trend suggests. Oxygen's fourth 2p electron shares one orbital and experiences extra electron–electron repulsion. Removing it relieves a pairing cost, whereas removing from nitrogen disrupts a stable singly occupied pattern.
Why not the others: (A) N is 2p³, not 2p⁶. (B) O is 2p⁴. (D) Both valence shells are n=2.
Key point: Consider orbital occupancy when a periodic trend has an exception.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A proton of mass m, charge e and alpha particle of mass 4m, charge 2e start from rest and traverse the same accelerating potential V nonrelativistically. Find λproton/λα.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) √8.
Given: Kinetic energy of each is qV; alpha mass and charge factors are 4 and 2.
Formula/Principle: λ=h/√(2mqV).
Step 1: pα²/pp²=(4m×2e)/(m×e)=8.
Step 2: Since λ is inverse momentum, λp/λα=√8.
Why: Equal potential does not mean equal kinetic energy for unequal charges. Kinetic gain is \(qV\), not simply \(V\). The alpha's doubled charge gives \(2eV\), while its fourfold mass controls speed through \(K=\tfrac12mv^2\); compare both before taking the speed ratio.
Why not the others: (A) takes only mass ratio's square root; (C) takes only charge ratio; (D) omits the square root.
Key point: Include both mass and charge in accelerated-particle momentum.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A+B→C uses 0.10 mol A and 0.16 mol B in a 1:1 reaction, isolating C at 80% theoretical yield. Then 2C→D isolates D at 75% of the theoretical yield from the isolated C. How many moles D result?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.030 mol.
Given: A limits the first reaction; the two yields apply successively.
Formula/Principle: Use stoichiometric ratios before applying each fractional yield.
Step 1: Theoretical C=0.10 mol, isolated C=0.10×0.80=0.080 mol.
Step 2: Theoretical D=0.080/2=0.040 mol, isolated D=0.040×0.75=0.030 mol.
Why: The second stage can use only C actually isolated, not the first stage's hypothetical maximum. The first reaction's limiting reactant fixes theoretical C, then the 80% isolation factor fixes usable C. The second reaction consumes that actual amount according to its 2:1 coefficient, so overall yield cannot be applied only at the end.
Why not the others: (A) misses the 2:1 step; (B) omits second yield; (C) applies yield without the reaction ratio.
Key point: Track material through each stage separately.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: At the para position, compare nitro- and methoxy-substituted benzoic acids with benzoic acid under the same conditions. Which is expected to be strongest?
options: A) p-Nitrobenzoic acid, because the electron-withdrawing group stabilises benzoate
B) p-Methoxybenzoic acid, because resonance donation stabilises benzoate
C) Benzoic acid, because substitution can never affect acidity
D) All exactly equal, because each has a COOH group
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) p-Nitrobenzoic acid.
Why: Nitro withdraws electron density through inductive and resonance effects and helps stabilise the negatively charged conjugate base. At para, methoxy resonance donation tends to oppose this stabilisation. Acid strength follows how favourably deprotonation products are stabilised under comparable conditions. A para nitro group withdraws through both induction and resonance, stabilising the carboxylate relative to neutral acid. A methoxy group donates by resonance at para, tending to destabilise that conjugate base in the relevant comparison.
Why not the others: (B) Donation does not stabilise the anion in the claimed way. (C) Ring substituents transmit electronic effects. (D) The same acidic group can have different environments.
Key point: Compare conjugate-base stabilisation, with substituent position specified.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows the two distinct carbonyl products from reductive ozonolysis of one acyclic alkene molecule, one molecule of each. Which alkene reconstructs the original carbon skeleton?
questions.image_alt: Two labelled product structures are methanal H–C(=O)–H and ethanal CH3–C(=O)–H; one of each forms per alkene.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Propene.
Why: Each carbonyl carbon was originally one carbon of the C=C bond. Rejoining the methanal carbon and ethanal carbon by a double bond, replacing their carbonyl oxygens, gives CH₂=CH–CH₃. The fragments account for all three carbons in propene. Reductive ozonolysis splits the C=C and puts one oxygen at each original alkene carbon. Reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons and removing the oxygens reconstructs the original carbon skeleton and substituent placement.
Why not the others: (A) Gives two methanals. (B) Gives two ethanals. (D) Gives methanal plus propanone rather than ethanal.
Key point: Reconstruct the two former alkene carbons from their separate carbonyl products.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Under mild conditions that permit ordinary SN2 substitution of a primary bromoalkane by hydroxide, bromobenzene is much less reactive. Which structural distinction matters most?
options: A) Bromobenzene has no C–Br bond
B) Resonance gives aryl C–Br partial double-bond character and sp² carbon disfavors backside SN2 attack
C) A primary bromoalkane has a benzene ring
D) Bromobenzene is freely ionised into phenyl cations in water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Aryl C–Br is resistant to ordinary SN2.
Why: Conjugation with the ring gives the C–Br bond partial double-bond character, and backside approach to an sp² aryl carbon is geometrically unfavourable. These features distinguish aryl from primary alkyl halides under the stipulated mild conditions. Ordinary SN2 requires attack at a tetrahedral carbon from behind the leaving group. Chlorobenzene binds Cl to sp² aryl carbon and has resonance-strengthened C–Cl character, so that mechanism is inaccessible under the mild comparison.
Why not the others: (A) The bond exists. (C) Primary bromoalkane is not aromatic. (D) Stable free phenyl cations do not form readily in water.
Key point: Do not transfer an alkyl-halide mechanism uncritically to an aryl halide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Phenol forms a salt with ordinary aqueous NaOH, whereas ethanol is not comparably deprotonated. What explains the difference?
options: A) Ethanol contains no O–H bond
C) Hydroxide reacts only with aromatic C–C bonds
D) Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised relative to an alkoxide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Phenoxide stabilisation.
Why: Deprotonating phenol gives an anion whose charge can delocalise into the aromatic system. Ethoxide lacks that resonance stabilisation, so ethanol is a substantially weaker acid under the usual qualitative comparison. Phenoxide has additional resonance contributors that spread its negative charge into the aromatic ring. Ethoxide is confined largely to oxygen, making its formation by aqueous hydroxide far less favourable.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanol has an O–H group. (B) Phenol is not an aldehyde. (C) The relevant reaction is proton transfer at oxygen.
Key point: Compare conjugate bases to explain an acidity contrast.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Charge of hydrolysed amino acids above pI
questions.question: Complete hydrolysis of Gly–Ala yields free glycine and alanine. At pH well above both isoelectric points, what net-charge tendency does each free amino acid have?
options: C) Glycine positive, alanine negative solely due to side chains
D) Both must be net neutral at every pH
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both tend net negative.
Why: Above each isoelectric point, deprotonation shifts the balance toward anionic forms. Glycine and alanine side chains do not introduce opposite ordinary ionisation behaviour, and hydrolysis frees their amino and carboxyl groups from the peptide bond. At high pH the carboxyl groups are deprotonated and the ammonium groups tend to lose protons. Evaluate each free amino acid's charge rather than assuming the intact peptide retains the same termini.
Why not the others: (B) Positive net charge is favoured at lower pH. (C) The non-ionising side chains do not reverse signs. (D) Net charge changes with pH.
Key point: Evaluate the free products at the stated pH, not the intact peptide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: AgCl has Ksp=1.0×10⁻¹⁰ at the stated temperature. Approximate equilibrium [Ag⁺] in 0.10 M NaCl if its dissolution changes [Cl⁻] negligibly.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.0×10⁻⁹ M.
Given: [Cl⁻]≈0.10 M from fully dissociated NaCl.
Formula/Principle: Ksp=[Ag⁺][Cl⁻] for AgCl(s).
Step 1: [Ag⁺]=10⁻¹⁰/0.10.
Step 2: This equals 10⁻⁹ M, far below added chloride and consistent with the approximation.
Why: Added chloride suppresses silver-ion concentration through the common-ion equilibrium. Write \(K_{\rm sp}=[\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]\). The added \(0.10\,\mathrm M\) chloride dominates the tiny chloride released by AgCl, so \([\mathrm{Ag^+}]\approx K_{\rm sp}/0.10\); check the resulting value is much smaller than 0.10 M.
Why not the others: (A) Is pure-water solubility; (B) omits division by chloride; (D) reports the chloride concentration.
Key point: Check the approximation after calculation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At fixed temperature and composition, a liquid mixture's total vapour pressure exceeds its ideal Raoult-law prediction. Which interaction pattern is consistent with this positive deviation?
options: A) Unlike A–B attractions must be stronger than like pairs
B) Unlike A–B attractions are weaker on average, permitting easier escape
C) The mixture has zero vapour pressure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Weaker unlike interactions.
Why: Mixing replaces some A–A and B–B neighbours with A–B neighbours. When those unlike contacts are less favourable on average, molecules escape more readily than the ideal reference predicts, raising total vapour pressure. Weaker unlike attractions make molecules escape more readily from the liquid than in the ideal mixture. A higher observed total vapour pressure is therefore a positive deviation; it does not imply that every component's mole fraction increased.
Why not the others: (A) Stronger unlike attractions generally cause negative deviation. (C) Contradicts pressure above a positive ideal prediction. (D) Positive deviation need not mean zero attraction.
Key point: Interpret vapour-pressure deviations through unlike contacts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Copper sulfate electrolysis with inert electrodes
questions.question: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with inert Pt electrodes under conditions where Cu²⁺ deposits at the cathode and water is oxidised at the anode. Which primary products follow?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Copper and oxygen.
Why: Cu²⁺ gains electrons at the cathode to form solid Cu. The stipulated anodic water oxidation releases O₂; sulfate remains in solution and does not become a gas. The electrode reactions must be assigned separately. At inert electrodes, the cathode and anode host separate reduction and oxidation half-reactions. Electrons consumed by Cu²⁺ deposition are balanced by electrons released from water oxidation under the specified conditions.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the specified copper deposition. (B) Sulfate reduction is not the anode reaction. (C) Gaseous sulfate is not an ordinary product.
Key point: Identify reduction and oxidation at their respective electrodes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M monoprotic acid and 50.0 mL of 0.500 M strong base react fully in an insulated calorimeter. The final 100 g solution warms 6.0 °C; use c=4.20 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect calorimeter heat. Assuming only neutralisation causes the measured heat, find enthalpy per mole water formed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −100.8 kJ/mol.
Given: Acid 0.0500 mol, base 0.0250 mol, so base limits and water formed is 0.0250 mol.
Formula/Principle: qsolution=mcΔT, qreaction=−qsolution.
Step 1: qsolution=100×4.20×6.0=2520 J.
Step 2: ΔH=−2.520 kJ/0.0250 mol=−100.8 kJ/mol water.
Why: The rising solution temperature means the reaction releases heat; dividing by the limiting amount fixes the molar basis. Equal solution mass and heat capacity turn the observed temperature rise into heat gained by solution. The reaction releases the opposite heat; divide by the actual limiting moles to report molar enthalpy with a negative sign.
Why not the others: (B) divides by all acid; (C) reverses heat sign; (D) halves reacting moles again.
Key point: Determine limiting product moles before normalising calorimetric heat.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Tangent-line parameter for an off-origin circle
questions.question: The circle x²+y²−6x−8y=0 is touched by a line 3x+4y=k. What are the possible values of k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0 and 50.
Given: Completing squares gives centre (3,4) and radius 5.
Formula/Principle: Tangency means centre-to-line distance equals radius.
Step 1: |3·3+4·4−k|/√(3²+4²)=5, hence |25−k|=25.
Step 2: k=0 or 50.
Worked derivation: \[(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=25,\quad \frac{|25-k|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=5\Longrightarrow |25-k|=25.\]
Why: The two parallel tangents lie on opposite sides of the circle, yielding both signs of the absolute-value equation. Both signs of the absolute value must be retained because the two parallel tangent lines touch opposite sides of the circle.
Why not the others: (A) centres the circle at origin; (B) omits the radius-normal factor; (C) mistakes the centre's line value for a tangent.
Key point: Translate to centre–radius form before using point-to-line distance.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The point (1,1) lies on x²+xy+y²=3. Where does its tangent meet the x-axis?
options: D) It is parallel to the x-axis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) x=2.
Given: Differentiating yields 2x+y+(x+2y)y′=0.
Formula/Principle: Implicit differentiation gives slope y′=−(2x+y)/(x+2y).
Step 1: At (1,1), slope=−3/3=−1.
Step 2: Tangent y−1=−(x−1), or x+y=2; set y=0 for x=2.
Worked derivation: \[2x+y+(x+2y)y'=0,\quad y'(1,1)=-1;\qquad y-1=-(x-1)\Longrightarrow x+y=2.\]
Why: The product xy contributes both y and xy′; dropping one term changes the intercept. The tangent is determined by both its slope and the given point. Setting y=0 only after writing the full line avoids mistaking the point's x-coordinate for the intercept.
Why not the others: (A) sign error in line; (B) reuses point coordinate; (D) ignores nonzero slope.
Key point: Derive slope first, then use the point to form the tangent.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Open-box volume optimisation with a feasible domain
questions.question: Equal squares of side x are cut from the four corners of a 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle, and the sides are folded into an open box. Which x gives maximum volume?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (10−2√7)/3 cm.
Given: Height x, base dimensions 12−2x and 8−2x, with feasible 0<x<4 cm.
Formula/Principle: V=x(12−2x)(8−2x)=4x(6−x)(4−x); maximise inside the physical interval.
Step 1: V′=4(24−20x+3x²). Setting it to zero gives x=(10±2√7)/3.
Step 2: The plus root exceeds 4 cm and is infeasible; the minus root lies inside (0,4), where V rises then falls. Endpoint volume tends to zero.
Worked derivation: \[V(x)=x(12-2x)(8-2x),\quad V'(x)=4(3x^2-20x+24)=0,\quad x=\frac{10\pm2\sqrt7}{3}.\]
Why: A stationary point outside the domain cannot describe a box, even if it solves the algebraic derivative equation. The feasible interval is 0<x<4. The larger root violates it, while V vanishes at both limiting endpoints and the derivative changes from positive to negative at the smaller root.
Why not the others: (A) is the invalid derivative root; (C) is feasible but not stationary; (D) collapses a base dimension to zero.
Key point: Optimisation needs both calculus and feasibility checks.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹[x/(1+x²)−x/(1+x)]dx.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (3/2)ln2−1.
Given: The two terms have different denominators and antiderivatives.
Formula/Principle: Substitute u=1+x² for the first; write x/(1+x)=1−1/(1+x) for the second.
Step 1: First integral=(1/2)ln2.
Step 2: Second integral=[x−ln(1+x)]₀¹=1−ln2.
Step 3: Difference=(3/2)ln2−1.
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^1\frac{x\,dx}{1+x^2}=\tfrac12\ln2,\quad\int_0^1\frac{x\,dx}{1+x}=1-\ln2,\quad I=\tfrac32\ln2-1>0.\]
Why: On 0<x<1, 1+x²<1+x, so the integrand is positive; the result is approximately +0.040, an independent sign check. The two antiderivatives require different substitutions. A numerical sign check agrees with the positive integrand on the interior, guarding against reversing the subtraction.
Why not the others: (B) reverses subtraction; (C) omits the second integral; (D) omits the substitution factor.
Key point: Integrate the two rational terms separately, then compare signs.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain of a composition with root and denominator
questions.question: Let f(x)=√(x−1) and g(t)=1/(t−2), both real-valued where defined. What is the domain of g∘f?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) x≥1 except 5.
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{dom}(f)=[1,\infty),\quad g(f(x))=\frac1{\sqrt{x-1}-2};\qquad \sqrt{x-1}=2\Longleftrightarrow x=5.\]
Why: The square root first requires x−1≥0. The outer function additionally forbids its input t=2; √(x−1)=2 occurs at x=5, which must be removed. Both conditions are needed to define the composition. The inner square root must be real before g can be evaluated. The outer denominator then removes a single otherwise valid point, not a whole interval.
Why not the others: (A) excludes valid x=1 and includes forbidden 5. (B) excludes valid 1≤x<5 and includes 5. (C) includes x<1 where the root is not real.
Key point: Apply inner-domain and outer-input constraints in order.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Scalar triple product with prescribed volume
questions.question: Vectors a=(1,1,0), b=(1,0,1), c=(t,1,1) span a parallelepiped of volume 3. What real t-values are possible?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −1 and 5.
Given: Volume is |a·(b×c)|.
Formula/Principle: b×c=(−1,t−1,1), hence a·(b×c)=t−2.
Step 1: Set |t−2|=3.
Step 2: Solve both signs: t−2=±3, giving t=5 or −1.
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf b\times\mathbf c=(-1,t-1,1),\quad \mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=t-2,\quad |t-2|=3\Longrightarrow t=-1,5.\]
Why: Volume loses orientation sign, so two distinct parameter values can create the same magnitude. Volume is an unsigned magnitude, so opposite orientations of the three vectors can have the same positive volume.
Why not the others: (A) Gives zero volume; (B) uses an incorrect centre for the absolute value; (D) misses the negative branch.
Key point: Do not discard either sign of an absolute scalar triple product.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A has rows R₁,R₂,R₃ and det A=3. Matrix B has rows R₁+R₂, R₂+R₃, R₃+R₁ in that order; then its first and third rows are interchanged. Find det B.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) −6.
Given: Before interchange, the row-combination matrix is T with rows (1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1).
Formula/Principle: det(TA)=det T·det A; one row interchange changes sign.
Step 1: Expand det T=1(1)−1(−1)=2, so intermediate determinant=2×3=6.
Step 2: Interchange first and third rows to obtain −6.
Worked derivation: \[\det T=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}=2,\quad\det(TA)=2(3)=6,\quad\det B=-6.\]
Why: These are three coupled row combinations, not three independent row additions that each preserve determinant. The simultaneous row combinations form a left multiplication with determinant two. The subsequent single row interchange changes sign once, independent of the row values.
Why not the others: (A) omits the final swap; (C) omits the transformation's factor 2; (D) omits both changes.
Key point: Represent simultaneous row combinations by a matrix before applying a later swap.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Three balls are drawn together from a bag with 4 red and 3 blue balls. Given that at least two drawn balls are red, what is the probability that all three are red?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/11.
Given: Three red draws=C(4,3)=4; exactly two red=C(4,2)C(3,1)=18.
Formula/Principle: Conditional probability is favourable count divided by count satisfying the condition.
Step 1: At least two red includes 18+4=22 selections.
Step 2: All three red probability=4/22=2/11.
Worked derivation: \[P(3R\mid\ge2R)=\frac{\binom43}{\binom42\binom31+\binom43}=\frac4{18+4}=\frac2{11}.\]
Why: After conditioning, the denominator is not all C(7,3)=35 possible samples. Conditioning discards all outcomes with fewer than two red balls. The numerator and denominator must count unordered three-ball samples in the same way.
Why not the others: (B) is unconditioned probability; (C) treats two event types as equally likely; (D) uses an incorrect favourable count.
Key point: Build the conditioned sample space before dividing.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A path from (0,0) to (5,4) uses only unit right or up steps. How many such paths avoid the point (2,2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 66.
Given: All paths use five right and four up steps.
Formula/Principle: Count all sequences then subtract those visiting the forbidden point.
Step 1: Total=C(9,4)=126. Paths to (2,2): C(4,2)=6; paths onward: C(5,2)=10.
Step 2: Through-point paths=6×10=60; avoiding=126−60=66.
Worked derivation: \[\binom94-\binom42\binom52=126-(6)(10)=66.\]
Why: The two subpaths can combine independently, which calls for multiplication before subtraction. A path through (2,2) decomposes uniquely into a path to that point and one from it to (5,4). These choices multiply; forbidden paths are then subtracted from all paths.
Why not the others: (A) ignores exclusion; (B) counts forbidden paths; (C) subtracts incorrectly.
Key point: Decompose paths at a required point and use complement for avoidance.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Vanishing coefficient followed by adjacent term
questions.question: For integer n≥4, the coefficient of x³ in (1+x)^n(1−x) vanishes. What is the coefficient of x⁴ in the same polynomial?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −5.
Given: Multiplication by 1−x makes coefficient of xʳ equal C(n,r)−C(n,r−1).
Formula/Principle: Set C(n,3)−C(n,2)=0; ratio C(n,3)/C(n,2)=(n−2)/3.
Step 1: (n−2)/3=1 gives n=5.
Step 2: x⁴ coefficient=C(5,4)−C(5,3)=5−10=−5.
Worked derivation: \[\binom n3=\binom n2\Longrightarrow \frac{n-2}{3}=1\Longrightarrow n=5;\qquad [x^4](1+x)^5(1-x)=\binom54-\binom53=-5.\]
Why: The vanishing x³ coefficient fixes the unknown exponent before the requested next coefficient can be evaluated. The vanishing coefficient determines n first. Only then can adjacent contributions to x⁴ be evaluated, with the minus sign from the factor (1−x) retained.
Why not the others: (A) reverses subtraction; (B) retains only the shifted term; (D) assumes the next coefficient also vanishes.
Key point: Convolution with a short factor relates adjacent binomial coefficients.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is Σₖ₌₁⁴ 1/[k(k+2)]?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 17/30.
Given: Four terms have denominators 3,8,15,24.
Formula/Principle: 1/[k(k+2)]=(1/2)(1/k−1/(k+2)).
Step 1: Telescoping leaves (1/2)(1+1/2−1/5−1/6).
Step 2: The bracket is 17/15, giving 17/30.
Worked derivation: \[\frac1{k(k+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1k-\frac1{k+2}\right),\quad S_4=\tfrac12(1+\tfrac12-\tfrac15-\tfrac16)=\frac{17}{30}.\]
Why: Interior reciprocal terms cancel after shifting by two. Writing out the first and last unmatched terms makes the shift-two telescoping visible and prevents the common error of cancelling too many boundary terms.
Why not the others: (A) stops at k=2; (C) stops at k=3; (D) accidentally sums 1/[k(k+1)] instead of the stated denominator.
Key point: Keep both unmatched terms at each end.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real k does x²−(k+1)x+(k−2)=0 have one negative root and one positive root strictly greater than 2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0<k<2.
Given: Root product k−2; polynomial value at x=2 is −k.
Formula/Principle: Opposite root signs require product<0. With an upward-opening parabola and negative root<0, x=2 lies between the roots precisely when p(2)<0.
Step 1: k−2<0 gives k<2.
Step 2: −k<0 gives k>0, ensuring positive root>2. Combine to 0<k<2.
Worked derivation: \[r_1r_2=k-2<0,\quad p(2)=2^2-2(k+1)+(k-2)=-k<0\Longrightarrow 0<k<2.\]
Why: At k=0 the positive root equals 2, while k=2 gives a zero root; both strict endpoints are excluded. For a monic quadratic with opposite-sign roots, p(2)<0 means 2 lies strictly between them and therefore below the positive root; equality at either endpoint fails the strict condition.
Why not the others: (B) includes values whose positive root is below 2; (C) includes forbidden endpoints; (D) loses opposite signs.
Key point: Combine Vieta's sign test with a polynomial-value test at the threshold.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Two equally sized groups have means 1 and 5 and population variances 4 and 4. What is the population variance when all observations are pooled?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8.
Given: Combined mean=(1+5)/2=3.
Formula/Principle: Pooled variance equals average within-group variance plus variance of group means about the combined mean.
Step 1: Within contribution=(4+4)/2=4.
Step 2: Between contribution=[(1−3)²+(5−3)²]/2=4; total=8.
Worked derivation: \[\mu=\frac{1+5}{2}=3,\quad \sigma^2=\frac{4+4}{2}+\frac{(1-3)^2+(5-3)^2}{2}=4+4=8.\]
Why: Groups have different centres, so averaging their individual variances alone omits between-group spread. The law of total variance has both within-group and between-group parts. Equal sizes make the group weights one-half but do not erase the separation between means.
Why not the others: (A) omits between-group spread; (B) averages shifts without squaring; (C) double-counts the shift.
Key point: Include both within- and between-group variation.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Eliminating constants from a solution family
questions.question: Which differential equation is satisfied by every function y=C₁e^x+C₂e^(−x), for arbitrary constants C₁,C₂?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) y″=y.
Worked derivation: \[y'=C_1e^x-C_2e^{-x},\qquad y''=C_1e^x+C_2e^{-x}=y.\]
Why: Differentiating once gives y′=C₁e^x−C₂e^(−x), so a first-order equation y′=y cannot accommodate the second term. Differentiating again restores the plus sign: y″=C₁e^x+C₂e^(−x)=y for all constants. Two independent constants remain free, so checking only a special choice such as C₂=0 would not establish an equation for the entire family.
Why not the others: (A) fails whenever C₂≠0. (B) reverses the second-derivative sign. (D) holds only for the zero function in this family.
Key point: Differentiate enough times to eliminate independent arbitrary constants.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Continuous extension and derivative at a point
questions.question: Define f(x)=sin(2x)/x for x≠0 and f(0)=k. For continuity at zero, what are k and f′(0)?
options: D) No value of k works
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) k=2 and derivative zero.
Given: sin(2x)/(2x)→1, hence f(x)→2.
Formula/Principle: Continuity fixes k=2; derivative is lim[x→0](sin2x/x−2)/x.
Step 1: Using sin2x=2x−(2x)³/6+o(x³), the numerator is −(4/3)x²+o(x²).
Step 2: Divide by x to obtain f′(0)=0.
Worked derivation: \[\sin(2x)=2x-\frac{(2x)^3}{6}+O(x^5),\quad f(x)=2-\frac43x^2+O(x^4),\quad k=2,\ f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)-2}{x}=0.\]
Why: A finite continuous value does not itself determine the derivative; a second limiting step is required. The continuous extension sets the value at zero; differentiability requires a separate difference quotient after cancellation, not just a repeated use of the first sine limit.
Why not the others: (A) fails continuity; (C) confuses limit with derivative; (D) ignores the standard sine limit.
Key point: Extend continuously before differentiating at a removable point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: From the same height, one ball is released horizontally and another is dropped from rest at the same instant. Neglect air resistance. Which lands first on level ground?
options: D) It depends on horizontal speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Simultaneously.
Worked derivation: \[y_1(t)=h-\tfrac12gt^2=y_2(t),\qquad t_{\rm hit}=\sqrt{2h/g}.\]
Why: Both start with zero vertical velocity and accelerate downward at g from the same height. Their vertical displacements are identical functions of time, while horizontal velocity changes only where the first ball lands. The horizontal launch changes x(t) but not the initial vertical velocity or vertical acceleration. This assumes air resistance is negligible and both are released at the same instant.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) incorrectly let horizontal motion alter fall time. (D) Horizontal speed affects range but not vertical flight time in this model.
Key point: Resolve projectile motion into independent components.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Instantaneous power as a dot product
questions.question: At an instant, v=(3î+4ĵ) m/s and force F=(2î−ĵ) N. What instantaneous power does this force supply?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 W.
Given: Both force and velocity are vectors with x and y components.
Formula/Principle: P=F·v, the rate of work along instantaneous motion.
Step 1: Multiply matching components: 2×3+(−1)×4=6−4.
Step 2: P=2 N·m/s=2 W.
Worked derivation: \[P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=(2)(3)+(-1)(4)=2\,{\rm N\,m\,s^{-1}}=2\,{\rm W}.\]
Why: The force's negative y component removes some of the power added by its x component. The dot product extracts force along instantaneous velocity; the negative y contribution cancels part of the positive x contribution.
Why not the others: (A) adds absolute contributions; (B) uses speed alone; (C) reverses the dot-product sign.
Key point: Power depends on the component of force along velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: The figure shows a uniform disc of original mass M and radius R with a circular hole of radius R/2 removed; its centre is R/2 from original centre O. About the perpendicular axis through O, what is the remaining moment of inertia?
questions.image_alt: An original disc centred at O has radius R; a circular hole of radius R/2 is centred at H, with OH=R/2, tangent to the original rim.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 13MR²/32.
Given: Uniform surface density makes removed mass M/4. The figure gives removed radius R/2 and displacement d=R/2.
Formula/Principle: Subtract the hole's inertia about O using the parallel-axis theorem.
Step 1: Original I=MR²/2; hole's central I=(M/4)(R/2)²/2=MR²/32.
Step 2: Hole's displacement term=(M/4)(R/2)²=MR²/16.
Step 3: Remaining I=MR²(1/2−1/32−1/16)=13MR²/32.
Worked derivation: \[m_{\rm hole}=M/4,\quad I_O^{\rm hole}=\tfrac12(M/4)(R/2)^2+(M/4)(R/2)^2=\frac{3MR^2}{32},\quad I_{\rm remain}=\frac{MR^2}{2}-I_O^{\rm hole}=\frac{13MR^2}{32}.\]
Why: The missing circle is not concentric with O, so subtracting only its central inertia is insufficient. The removed circle contributes its own central inertia plus a parallel-axis shift about O. Using the final remaining mass M in the full-disc formula would change the meaning of M in the stem.
Why not the others: (A) mishandles removed mass; (B) omits part of parallel-axis shift; (D) treats the hole as central.
Key point: Treat removed material as a negative body at the same axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Free-surface slope in an accelerating tank
questions.question: An open water tank accelerates to the right at g/2. In its frame, what is the magnitude of the steady free-surface slope, vertical rise divided by horizontal distance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: Effective gravity is g down plus g/2 left.
Formula/Principle: A free surface is perpendicular to effective gravity; |Δh/Δx|=a/g.
Step 1: Substitute a=g/2.
Step 2: Slope magnitude=(g/2)/g=1/2; it is higher on the left.
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf g_{\rm eff}=-(g/2)\hat{\mathbf x}-g\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \left|\frac{dh}{dx}\right|=\frac{g/2}{g}=\frac12.\]
Why: In the accelerating frame, the horizontal pseudo acceleration tilts the effective gravity vector. The free surface is perpendicular to effective gravity. The horizontal fictitious acceleration points left in the tank frame, making the fluid higher on that side.
Why not the others: (A) inverts a/g; (C) assumes a=g; (D) squares the ratio.
Key point: Separate the slope magnitude from its left-right direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two identical bodies of constant heat capacity C start at absolute temperatures T and 3T. Isolated together, they equilibrate without work. What is their total entropy change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C ln(4/3).
Given: Energy balance gives final temperature (T+3T)/2=2T.
Formula/Principle: For each body, ΔS=C ln(Tfinal/Tinitial).
Step 1: Add C ln(2T/T)+C ln(2T/3T).
Step 2: Combine to C ln(4/3)>0.
Worked derivation: \[2CT_f=C(T+3T)\Longrightarrow T_f=2T;\quad \Delta S=C\ln\frac{2T}{T}+C\ln\frac{2T}{3T}=C\ln\frac43.\]
Why: Equal and opposite heat transfer between bodies still creates net entropy when it occurs across a finite temperature difference. Both bodies share one isolated final temperature from energy balance. Entropy changes must be calculated separately for hot and cold bodies before adding; zero net heat does not mean zero entropy production.
Why not the others: (B) confuses zero net heat with zero entropy; (C) reverses the logarithm; (D) ignores the hot body's entropy loss.
Key point: Sum each body's state-function change.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: At a fixed instant, two points along a sinusoidal travelling wave are separated by λ/6 in the propagation direction. What is their phase difference modulo 2π?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) π/3.
Given: One full wavelength corresponds to 2π spatial phase.
Formula/Principle: Δφ=2πΔx/λ.
Step 1: Substitute Δx=λ/6.
Step 2: Δφ=2π/6=π/3.
Worked derivation: \[\phi(x,t)=kx-\omega t+\phi_0,\quad |\Delta\phi|=k\Delta x=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\frac{\lambda}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3}.\]
Why: Comparing positions at the same instant isolates the spatial phase term rather than time evolution. Comparing two positions at the same instant cancels the time-dependent term. The result is a phase difference, not a path length or a time delay.
Why not the others: (A) omits the factor two; (B) uses a quarter wavelength; (C) doubles the result.
Key point: Convert displacement to phase as a fraction of a full cycle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Total energy of a circular satellite orbit
questions.question: A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M in a circle of radius r. Taking potential energy zero at infinity, what is its total mechanical energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −GMm/(2r).
Given: The circular-orbit condition gives mv²/r=GMm/r².
Formula/Principle: K=mv²/2=GMm/(2r), U=−GMm/r.
Step 1: Add K and U.
Step 2: E=GMm/(2r)−GMm/r=−GMm/(2r).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^2}\Longrightarrow K=\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{2r};\quad E=K+U=\frac{GMm}{2r}-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{GMm}{2r}.\]
Why: The negative result signifies a bound orbit relative to zero energy at infinity. Circular orbit fixes speed through gravity; gravitational potential energy remains negative with zero chosen at infinity. The total bound energy is half the potential energy, not the same quantity.
Why not the others: (A) loses binding sign; (B) reports U alone; (D) falsely equates kinetic and potential magnitudes.
Key point: Total energy is not the same as gravitational potential energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Zero potential on a signed line
questions.question: The figure places +q at x=0 and −4q at x=3a, with a>0. At which finite points on the x-axis is the electric potential zero?
questions.image_alt: On a signed horizontal axis, +q is at x=0 and −4q is at x=3a, with the separation labelled 3a and a>0.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) −a and 3a/5.
Given: The signed-axis diagram fixes charge positions and two sign-change intervals.
Formula/Principle: V=kq/|x|−4kq/|x−3a|=0, hence |x−3a|=4|x|.
Step 1: For x<0, 3a−x=−4x gives x=−a.
Step 2: For 0<x<3a, 3a−x=4x gives x=3a/5; for x>3a, the formal solution fails that interval.
Worked derivation: \[\frac1{|x|}=\frac4{|x-3a|}\Longleftrightarrow |x-3a|=4|x|;\quad x<0:\ x=-a,\quad 0<x<3a:\ x=3a/5.\]
Why: Potential is scalar but distances remain positive, so absolute values need separate intervals. Distances must remain nonnegative in each region, and neither charge location is a valid finite-potential point. A formal root outside the interval assumed to derive it must be rejected.
Why not the others: (A) uses equal charge magnitudes; (C) names singular charge positions; (D) chooses distances with incorrect interval signs.
Key point: Verify every algebraic solution in its positional interval.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Plate separation change at fixed battery voltage
questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to an ideal constant-voltage battery while plate separation is doubled, with area and dielectric unchanged. How do stored charge and energy change?
options: C) Charge halves but energy doubles
D) Charge stays fixed and energy halves
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both become half.
Worked derivation: \[C_i=\frac{\varepsilon A}{d},\quad C_f=\frac{\varepsilon A}{2d}=\frac{C_i}{2};\qquad Q_f=C_fV=\frac{Q_i}{2},\quad U_f=\tfrac12C_fV^2=\frac{U_i}{2}.\]
Why: Capacitance εA/d halves when d doubles. The connected ideal battery holds V fixed, so Q=CV and U=CV²/2 each scale with C and halve. The battery can accept the charge that leaves the capacitor. The connected ideal battery fixes voltage but permits charge exchange. Applying Q constant would describe a disconnected capacitor and produce a different energy trend.
Why not the others: (B) Reverses capacitance change. (C) Assigns different scaling to quantities both proportional to C at fixed V. (D) Treats an attached battery as if it were disconnected.
Key point: Identify the fixed voltage boundary condition before applying capacitance formulas.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω supplies a 4 Ω external resistor. What is the terminal voltage while it delivers current?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8 V.
Given: Total series resistance 6 Ω.
Formula/Principle: I=E/(R+r), Vterminal=IR=E−Ir.
Step 1: I=12/6=2 A.
Step 2: Terminal voltage=2×4=8 V.
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}=\frac{12}{4+2}=2\,{\rm A};\qquad V_{\rm terminal}=IR=(2)(4)=8\,{\rm V}=\mathcal E-Ir.\]
Why: Two volts of internal resistance at 2 A account for 4 V dropped inside the cell. The internal resistor dissipates Ir=4 V at this current, so the external terminal voltage is below the open-circuit emf.
Why not the others: (A) assumes no internal drop; (B) reports that drop; (C) treats resistance sum as voltage.
Key point: Distinguish emf from voltage under load.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The plane of a single-turn loop of area A carrying current I makes 30° with a uniform magnetic field B. What is the torque magnitude?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (√3/2)IAB.
Given: Loop normal makes 60° with the field.
Formula/Principle: Torque magnitude=IAB sinθ, where θ is normal–field angle.
Step 1: θ=90°−30°=60°.
Step 2: τ=IAB sin60°=(√3/2)IAB.
Worked derivation: \[\theta_{\mu B}=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ,\qquad \tau=\mu B\sin\theta_{\mu B}=IAB\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}IAB.\]
Why: The magnetic moment is normal to the loop's plane, so the stated plane angle is not directly θ. Torque depends on the angle between the field and the loop's normal, which is the magnetic moment direction, not the given plane–field angle.
Why not the others: (A) substitutes 30°; (B) assumes 90°; (D) assumes alignment of normal and field.
Key point: Convert a plane angle to the dipole-axis angle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal transformer has 200 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. Its primary is at 240 V rms; the secondary drives a 6 Ω resistive load. What are secondary voltage and primary current?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 60 V and 2.5 A.
Given: Turns ratio Ns/Np=1/4 and secondary resistor 6 Ω.
Formula/Principle: Vs/Vp=Ns/Np; ideal input power equals output power.
Step 1: Vs=240/4=60 V; Is=Vs/R=10 A.
Step 2: VpIp=VsIs=600 W, so Ip=600/240=2.5 A.
Worked derivation: \[V_s=240\frac{50}{200}=60\,{\rm V},\quad I_s=\frac{60}{6}=10\,{\rm A},\quad I_p=\frac{V_sI_s}{V_p}=\frac{600}{240}=2.5\,{\rm A}.\]
Why: Lower voltage accompanies higher secondary current for conserved power. Ideal power conservation connects currents on different windings; the load current is not the same as the supply current of a step-down transformer.
Why not the others: (A) reports secondary current as primary; (C) ignores turns ratio; (D) uses a half instead of quarter ratio.
Key point: Combine turns ratio with load and power conservation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Optical path excess through a slab
questions.question: A ray crosses a slab of thickness L normally, refractive index n. Relative to the same geometric distance in vacuum, what is excess optical path length?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (n−1)L.
Given: Slab path length L and refractive index n.
Formula/Principle: Optical path is n times geometric distance in that medium.
Step 1: Slab optical path=nL; vacuum path=L.
Step 2: Excess=nL−L=(n−1)L.
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{OPL}_{\rm slab}=nL,\quad\mathrm{OPL}_{\rm vacuum}=L,\qquad\Delta\mathrm{OPL}=nL-L=(n-1)L.\]
Why: The question asks for a comparison, so total slab optical path alone is not the final answer. The excess compares two paths of the same geometric length. Referencing the vacuum path avoids mistaking the slab's total optical length for the requested difference.
Why not the others: (B) is total path; (C) is not the defined optical path; (D) adds instead of subtracts the reference.
Key point: Subtract the specified baseline from optical path.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Propagation from E and B orientation
questions.question: An electromagnetic plane wave has electric field along +y and magnetic field along +z. What direction does it propagate?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +x.
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf S\ \parallel\ \mathbf E\times\mathbf B,\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}.\]
Why: Energy transport and propagation follow the Poynting direction E×B. For a right-handed coordinate system, ŷ×ẑ=x̂, perpendicular to both fields. The Poynting vector defines energy-flow direction in a plane wave; reversing cross-product order would reverse propagation, and propagation is perpendicular to both fields.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses cross-product order. (B) and (C) put propagation along one field, whereas a plane electromagnetic wave is transverse.
Key point: Use field orientation, not field magnitude, for propagation direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Two half-lives: activity and surviving fraction
questions.question: Equal initial numbers N₀ of nuclides X and Y have half-lives 2 h and 4 h. After 8 h, find (i) activity ratio AX:AY and (ii) fraction of all initial nuclei still undecayed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1:2 and 5/32.
Given: X has undergone four half-lives, leaving N₀/16; Y two, leaving N₀/4.
Formula/Principle: Activity A=λN with λ=ln2/T½; total survivor fraction=(NX+NY)/(2N₀).
Step 1: λX/λY=2, so AX/AY=2(1/16)/(1/4)=1/2.
Step 2: Surviving fraction=(1/16+1/4)/2=5/32.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{N_X}{N_0}=2^{-8/2}=\frac1{16},\quad\frac{N_Y}{N_0}=2^{-8/4}=\frac14;\quad \frac{A_X}{A_Y}=\frac{\lambda_XN_X}{\lambda_YN_Y}=\frac{2(1/16)}{1/4}=\frac12,\quad \frac{N_X+N_Y}{2N_0}=\frac5{32}.\]
Why: More X nuclei have decayed, but its decay constant is twice as large, so population ratio alone is not activity ratio. Activity depends on both survivor count and decay constant. The two initial populations contribute equally to the denominator of the overall survival fraction.
Why not the others: (A) uses population ratio as activity; (B) reverses it; (D) reports the decayed fraction.
Key point: Keep population and activity distinct for each isotope.
